notes.1a: Many candidates gave the correct answer. Some candidates made errors with counting on and subtracting, often losing or gaining one hour. Candidates could be encouraged to draw a careful time line to show whether to add or subtract.
notes.1bi: Most candidates gave the correct answer. A small number of candidates made arithmetic errors.
notes.1bii: Many candidates gave the correct answer. Some candidates gave an answer of 85% with no working. Since the general rubric requires three significant figures, these candidates lost marks.
notes.1biii: A substantial number of candidates gave the correct answer. A few candidates gave an answer of 96.28 .
notes.1c: A few candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was to assume that ‘correct to the nearest metre’ meant the answer was ±1 of the given number, rather than ±0.5. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2015 (d) (i) Most candidates gave the correct answers in the correct spaces.
notes.1cii: Generally all candidates drew the bar chart and completed the scale on the frequency axis very carefully. Some candidates did not choose the most appropriate scale to enable accurate bars to be drawn. Candidates need to be encouraged to look at the largest frequency and work out how high this could sensibly go up the y- axis. Most candidates were careful in ensuring the bars had equal gaps or widths.
notes.2a: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer, with or without working. Candidates should be aware that there is no ability to gain part marks when no working is shown. The common method errors were to divide 21 600 by 2 then 3 then 4, or to just divide 21 600 into 3 equal parts.
notes.2bi: Many candidates gave the correct answer. The main error seen was copying 14 000 inaccurately as 1400. Candidates should be encouraged to look at their answers in general to check for inaccurate copying.
notes.2bii: Most candidates gave the correct answer. The common error was to not simplify the fraction to its lowest form as required.
notes.2biii: Some candidates gave the correct answer. Many candidates did not take off all of the parts, 4200, 8000 and 600.
notes.2c: A large number of candidates gave the correct answer. The common errors were only calculating 17280 × 100 = 80% or dividing by 17 280 to reach 25%. 21600 (d) Although there were a few correct answers given, a number of candidates did not answer this part. Those candidates that did attempt this part generally used compound interest. The most common errors were to either round too soon, losing accuracy, or to give 5922.89 as the answer. Some candidates accurately found the interest each year but omitted the final step of adding them together.
notes.3ai: For those candidates who tried to plot the points, most plotted all 4 points accurately, with the rest plotting 3 accurately. Some candidates did not plot the extra four points.
notes.3aii: Most candidates attempted this part, even those who had not plotted the points in part (a)(i) . Candidates would benefit from having further practice at drawing lines of best fit. Care should be taken that a balance of points occurs on each side of the line. Some candidates joined all the points. It should be emphasised that the line does not need to go through the end points of the data.
notes.3aiii: Many candidates gave ‘negative’ correctly as their answer. Some candidates embellished this further with terms such as ‘weak’ or ‘strong’.
notes.3bi: Most candidates picked out the correct point but some gave the x -value instead of the y -value.
notes.3bii: Many candidates, with or without a correct line of best fit, were able to come up with a sensible answer. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2015
notes.4ai: Candidates generally gave the correct answer. The common error was to incorrectly change the signs of terms when moving from one side of an equation to another. The most common incorrect answers were 47 and –11.
notes.4aii: Candidates generally gave the correct answer. The common errors included 8 y + 24 = 164, 8 y + 28 = 656 and 2 y + 7 = 164 – 4. (b) Most candidates gave the correct answer. The most common errors were 48 x , or trying to factorise.
notes.4ci: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.4cii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.4ciii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. The common incorrect answers were 8 and 0.
notes.4di: Many candidates gave the correct answer. A few gave answers of 6700 or 7000 or 680.
notes.4dii: Nearly every candidate gave the correct answer. A few candidates gave a percentage instead of a fraction. It is essential that candidates read the question carefully to see how the answer should be displayed.
notes.4diii: Nearly every candidate gave the correct answer. The most common errors included 60, 0.06%, 100 (iv) Most candidates gave the correct answer. The common error was 687 × 10 . 5 8
notes.5ai: Many of the candidates gave the correct answer, although ‘radio’ and ‘ratio’ were seen commonly.
notes.5aii: Very few candidates answered this correctly. Incorrect words included ‘diameter’, ‘segment’, ‘tangent’ and ‘rope’.
notes.5bi: Candidates struggled with the reasons in this part. Of those who knew the reasons, it was more common to show a calculation than give the reason in words. A number of candidates measured the angles. Few used the word ‘semi-circle’.
notes.5biii: Follow through marks were awarded a number of times. The reason was very rarely correct.
notes.5biv: Follow through marks were awarded a number of times. The reason was given correctly a few times. 180° (iii) 65° angle [between] radius and tangent is 90° (iv) 65° alternate angles Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2015
notes.6ai: Many candidates gave the correct colour.
notes.6aii: The common error in this part was to use an incorrect radius, 0.9 instead of 1.5. There was evidence of premature approximation in the working. A substantial number of candidates did not give an answer.
notes.6aiii: Many candidates gave the correct answer. Some candidates forgot to find the change, only working out the amount spent. 16
notes.7ai: A substantial number of candidates gave the correct answer. There were few arithmetic errors and no clear apparent common error.
notes.7aii: Some candidates obtained the correct answer following an incorrect answer in the previous part, suggesting that candidates may have started again.
notes.7bi: A large majority of candidates measured the length accurately and converted it using the given scale.
notes.7bii: Most candidates produced clear accurate diagrams. A common error was to shade the wrong area. A few candidates did not answer this part.
notes.7biii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. Some candidates did not convert properly, for example, 0.00065.
notes.8a: A few candidates gave the correct answer. Most candidates were unable to find the gradient and others misunderstood the different scales on the two axes.
notes.8bi: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. However, many candidates calculated the values involving negative signs incorrectly.
notes.8bii: The majority of candidates carefully plotted and drew the curve smoothly. There was little evidence of joining the points with straight lines.
notes.8biii: Some good responses were seen, with scales read accurately. However, a common error was to read the scale backwards from ‘–1’, so instead of –0.4, –1.6 or similar was seen. A few candidates used the quadratic formula and tried to answer this algebraically. They often gave roots that were very accurate but commonly both positive, or the signs the wrong way round. notes.9ai: Many candidates gave a correctly rotated triangle. Some, however, used the wrong centre.
notes.9aii: Some candidates drew the correct reflection. However, a few candidates reflected the triangle in x = k or y = –1.
notes.9aiii: Candidates found this part particularly challenging. Only a few gained full marks. The centre of enlargement was often inaccurately stated due to drawing lines from shapes and writing (7.5, 3.5) or (4,7). The scale factor was often stated as ‘half the size’.
notes.9bi: Candidates generally gave the correct answer but sometimes gave answers such as (5, 2) or (–5, –2).
notes.9bii: Although some candidates gave the correct answer, many had problems with the signs in the vector. Some candidates wrote the previous answer as a column vector.

notes.10a: Nearly all candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.10bi: Although many candidates gave the correct answer, a few gave a numerical answer rather than an expression in terms of n . The most common error was n + 5.
notes.10bii: Those candidates who wrote 5 n for part (b)(i) generally got this right. Very few candidates who got part (b)(i) incorrect realised that they needed to add 1 to the previous answer.
